doc.title: Phoebe Jacobs and Jackie Harris interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 21, 2006

title: Preserving New Orleans heritage and founding the jazz camp
summary: Harris explains the festival's mission of preserving legacy while teaching youth, and why she created the jazz camp and wants jazz history taught as American history.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: When you started doing the Jazz & Heritage work was there a directive or a sense of what part of our heritage are we trying to cover here? Because there’s so much in New Orleans. Did you have to balance new with old?

Well but you know that’s what New Orleans music is all about. You know it’s about preserving the cultural legacy of New Orleans and its music and the people that created that music while at the same time we are driven and feel that it is imperative that we teach young people about that music. I mean it’s the only way it’s going to continue to live on.

Well that’s what, you know I felt that any young person that had an interest or a gift and wanted to learn jazz music in the city where it was created should have the opportunity to do so, whether they lived in New Orleans, whether they lived in Louisiana, in other states or in other countries. And if we are the birthplace of jazz, as we are, I think that it’s incumbent upon us to, and if we’re saying that we’re trying to preserve this legacy, we must teach the young people about the people that created this music. And learning to play the music is very important. But you know the history of this music is American history. It’s America’s true and only art form. And so Phoebe and I are working together to try to get the story of the creation of jazz and these pioneers and heroes as part of what young people learn in American history.
